To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the development of breast cancer in rats is influenced by the strain of rats, that hormone-responsive tumours can become hormone-unresponsive during the transplant procedure and that this change in the hormone-response is accompanied by a change in the histological structure of the tumour.

(i) the hormone-response of the induced rat mammary tumours was dependent on ovarian function; (ii) the hormone-response could be changed by transplanting hormone-responsive tumours; (iii) this change in hormone-responsiveness was not caused by a transformation of the original tumour, but by selection of a hormone-unresponsive tumour cell population; and (iv) the change in hormone-responses was paralleled by morphological changes in the tumour.
the hormone-responsiveness of the transplantable tumours was changed from hormone-dependent to hormone-unresponsive during the transplantation procedure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a rat model for the investigation of the mechanisms of hormone-responsiveness in breast cancer.
the study of the development of hormone-responsiveness of transplantable breast tumours.
the study of hormone-response of transplantable breast tumours.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a selection of hormone-responsive tumour cells takes place during transplantation, resulting in the selection of a hormone-independent tumour cell population.
the hormone-response in the breast cancers induced by DMBA was dependent upon the hormonal environment in the animal.
a change in hormone-response is not an intrinsic characteristic of the tumour cell but a selection phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hormone-response of breast tumours in the rat is a dynamic process, and that the hormone-responsiveness is a characteristic of the tumour as a whole rather than a property of the individual cell.
the hormone-response of a transplantable breast cancer can be influenced by the hormone status of the animal in which it grows.
the hormone-response in breast cancer is not a stable phenomenon and that this instability can be observed in vivo as well as in vitro.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the change in hormone response is not an artefact due to the transplantation procedure, but a real phenomenon which is related to the morphology and growth pattern of the tumour.
hormone-responsive tumours can be induced and transplanted in rats, and that this system may be a suitable model to study the development of hormone resistance.
hormone-responsive transplantable breast tumours are a valuable model for studying mechanisms underlying the development of hormone resistance in breast cancer.
